title: Polynomial-time private release of all marginals
formal: Do there exist an integer \(C\ge1\), a function \(\alpha:\mathbb N_{\ge2}\to[0,1]\) with \(\lim_{d\to\infty}\alpha(d)=0\), a uniform randomized mechanism \(M\), and a uniform deterministic evaluator \(E\) satisfying the following statement? For every integer \(d\ge2\), put \(n=d^{C}\). For every explicitly given database \(D\in(\{0,1\}^{d})^{n}\), \(M(d,D)\) runs in worst-case time polynomial in \(n+d\), satisfies \((1,1/(100n^{2}))\)-differential privacy under replacement of one row, and outputs a finite binary synopsis \(S\). With probability at least \(2/3\) over \(M\)'s random bits, this one synopsis satisfies \[\left|E(d,S,J,a)-q_{J,a}(D)\right|\le\alpha(d)\] simultaneously for every \(J\subseteq[d]\) and \(a\in\{0,1\}^{J}\). The evaluator runs in worst-case time polynomial in \(d+|S|\), outputs a binary-encoded rational, and has no further access to the database. The synopsis may be arbitrary: it need not be synthetic data or describe a consistent probability distribution.
definitions: \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\). A marginal query \((J,a)\) asks for the fraction of rows agreeing with the assignment \(a\) on the coordinates in \(J\): \[q_{J,a}(D)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf 1\{\forall j\in J,\ D_{ij}=a_j\}.\] All orders \(0\le|J|\le d\) are included; the empty query equals one. Each query can be encoded as a length-\(d\) word over \(\{*,0,1\}\), indicating omitted coordinates or required bits; fix any constant-length binary encoding of these symbols. Thus there are \(3^{d}\) queries with descriptions of length \(O(d)\). The database is an ordered \(n\)-by-\(d\) bit matrix. For every ordered pair of equal-size databases \(D,D'\) differing at one row and every set \(O\) of binary output strings, privacy requires \[\Pr[M(d,D)\in O]\le e\Pr[M(d,D')\in O]+1/(100n^{2}).\] It is a guarantee on the whole synopsis distribution. \(M\) and \(E\) are ordinary classical multitape Turing machines with no advice, oracle or shared private database state; \(M\) uses independent fair bits. One fixed polynomial bounds its time, output length and number of random bits on every execution. One fixed polynomial bounds the evaluator's time on every valid query and synopsis. The probability of simultaneous accuracy is required separately for every database, with no input-distribution promise. All of \(C,\alpha,M,E\) and their polynomial bounds are chosen before \(d,D\). The convergence condition means that for every real \(\eta>0\), there is \(d_0\) such that \(\alpha(d)\le\eta\) for all \(d\ge d_0\); no computable convergence rate or procedure for evaluating \(\alpha\) is required. Error is an absolute error in a row fraction in \([0,1]\), not in the unnormalized count. These are the concrete synopsis, privacy and sample-size conventions already selected for this card in September 2026; they are not claimed equivalent to every interactive or fixed-order variant of the source question.
answer_criterion: Prove this existence statement or its logical negation in Lean. A positive answer must exhibit the fixed uniform machines, exponent, polynomial resource bounds and vanishing error function and prove both privacy and simultaneous accuracy on every valid database. A negative answer must exclude all such choices; hardness only under an unproved cryptographic assumption proves the corresponding conditional obstruction, not the unconditional negation. Fixed positive error, accuracy only for most queries or typical databases, a polynomial number of interactive queries, or a runtime polynomial in the exponential number of all query answers does not meet the stated criterion. The target is the existence of a vanishing-error polynomial-time synopsis, rather than a numerical value requiring additive \(1/100\) determination.
why: Marginals are basic summaries of relationships among attributes. The question asks whether the large information-theoretic usefulness of private high-dimensional data can be captured by a compact, efficiently evaluated object using polynomially many records. It isolates a statistical-versus-computational gap for a concrete query family while allowing outputs more flexible than synthetic datasets.

importance.reason: A fundamental statistical-versus-computational gap for a concrete and widely used query family. It complements existing sample-complexity questions and has an explicit specialist open-problem formulation, while allowing non-synthetic outputs avoids a known source of misleading hardness claims.

progress.text: The checked 2013 manuscript, published at ITCS 2014, gives subexponential per-query private marginal answers for small databases at fixed absolute error.
Open Problem 7.8 in the March author manuscript explicitly asks for polynomial-time estimation of every higher-order marginal with vanishing error and polynomially many records.

Weighted Fourier factorizations give optimal Gaussian-factorization variance for arbitrary specified marginal workloads with runtime polynomial in explicit output size; this does not bound the time or synopsis size polynomially in dimension for all marginals.

Rechecked the source’s exact open question, the older interactive theorem and the recent output-size-dependent algorithm. No matching polynomial all-marginal synopsis or unconditional impossibility was found in the bounded later-work search.

context_blocks.text: A marginal measures how often a selected pattern occurs in a set of attributes. Low-order queries concern small attribute groups; this problem includes every order. There are exponentially many queries, but each query has a short description. Polynomial running time therefore requires a reusable compact synopsis with a query evaluator, rather than an explicit table of all answers.

Privacy and accuracy concern different quantifiers. Changing one person’s entire row must leave the output distribution nearly unchanged. For each fixed database, a single successful synopsis must answer every query accurately at once. Evaluating it after release accesses no additional records. A guarantee for each query separately with a fresh failure probability would not give the requested simultaneous event.

Vadhan’s 2017 open question asks for vanishing error with polynomially many records and polynomial computation. The current card retains the previously approved approximate-privacy parameters and a noninteractive binary synopsis. The survey’s alternative question about some growing but restricted order is not substituted for the all-orders requirement.

Chandrasekaran, Thaler, Ullman and Wan give a subexponential per-query algorithm on small databases. Theorem 1.1 handles a sequence of adaptively chosen marginal queries at fixed absolute error and its database-size guarantee depends on the length of that sequence. This is meaningful progress, but is not a polynomial-time construction of one synopsis answering all orders with vanishing error.

The survey’s synthetic-data hardness theorem assumes one-way functions and restricts the output to a new database, even for two-way marginals. It does not rule out an arbitrary synopsis: the survey explicitly contrasts that obstruction with efficient nonsynthetic answers to low-order marginals. The benchmark deliberately retains this broader output interface.

The checked December 2025 weighted-Fourier paper provides exact optimality for weighted or maximum noise variance within Gaussian factorization mechanisms. Its runtime is polynomial in the dataset and the explicit output/workload size. For the entire \(3^{d}\)-query family that size is exponential, and variance optimality within that mechanism class is not a general polynomial-synopsis theorem or impossibility result.

source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase

sentences: A marginal query asks what fraction of database rows match a pattern on selected attributes.
The card asks for one private synopsis that answers all exponentially many such queries with error tending to zero as the dimension grows.
Both creating the synopsis and evaluating a short query must use polynomial time, with only polynomially many input rows.
Known interactive, synthetic-data and Gaussian-factorization results impose different resource or output requirements and do not settle this target.
A complete Lean answer must prove the specified uniform existence statement or rule out every mechanism and evaluator satisfying it.
